a2z-406.description:
A frog stands on stone 0 of n stones with heights h[0..n-1]; it may jump 1 or 2 stones forward, paying |h[i] - h[j]| energy per jump. Find the minimum total energy to reach stone n-1. (Classic 1D DP introduction.)

dp[i] = minimum energy to stand on stone i: dp[0] = 0, dp[1] = |h1-h0|, and dp[i] = min(dp[i-1] + |h[i]-h[i-1]|, dp[i-2] + |h[i]-h[i-2]|). O(n) time; reduce to two rolling variables for O(1) space. Recursion + memo is the teaching path, tabulation the expected answer.
constraints: O(n) time; O(1) space with rolling variables

a2z-407.description:
Extend the frog jump: the frog can now jump any distance from 1 to k stones ahead, still paying |h[i] - h[j]| per jump. Minimum energy to reach the last of n stones.

dp[i] = min over j = 1..min(k, i) of dp[i-j] + |h[i] - h[i-j]|. O(n·k) time — the k = 2 case is the previous exercise. Space O(n) for the table, or a sliding window of k values for O(k). Reading input: T test cases with n, k, then heights.

A monotone-queue trick (two deques tracking dp[j] ± h[j]) can reach O(n), but the sheet expects the direct O(n·k) recurrence.

a2z-410.description:
Ninja has N days and three tasks (A, B, C); points[d][t] is the points earned doing task t on day d. Each day he does exactly one task, and the same task cannot be done on two consecutive days. Maximize total points over the N days.

State = (day, last task done): dp[d][t] = points[d][t] + max over t' ≠ t of dp[d-1][t']. Base: day 0 is just points[0][t]. Answer = max over t of dp[N-1][t]. O(N·3·2) time; the 'can't repeat yesterday' constraint lives entirely in the last-task state — the lesson of the problem. Space reduces to the previous row (or 4 variables).

a2z-415.description:
A grid of N rows × M columns holds cherries (0..1000 per cell). Three ninjas start at the top row — columns 0, M/2 (middle) and M-1 — and descend to the bottom row; from (r, c) each may move to (r+1, c-1), (r+1, c) or (r+1, c+1). When two or three land on the same cell, its cherries are collected once. Maximize total cherries collected.

DP over rows with the column triple as state: dp[c1][c2][c3] = best total up to the current row with the ninjas at those columns. Transition enumerates all 3³ = 27 next-column combinations, adding the cherries of the distinct target cells (the 'collect once' rule handled by deduplicating the up-to-3 columns). O(N·M³·27); memory two rows. Without the sharing rule the problem would split into three independent path DPs — the coupling is the point.

examples.explanation: Row 0 collects 2+3+1 = 6; best spread on row 1 is columns 0,1,2 again (all can reach their own column): 1+5+1 = 7; total 13.
One row: start positions are the answer, all distinct.

constraints: 1 <= N <= 100, 3 <= M <= 20 (M odd so a middle column exists)
O(N·M³) time, O(M³) or two-row space

a2z-416.description:
Given an array of positive integers and a target sum, decide whether some subset sums exactly to the target. Return true/false (0/1).

Subset-sum is the 0/1 knapsack decision form: dp[i][s] = using first i items, can sum s be made? Transitions: skip (dp[i-1][s]) or take (dp[i-1][s - arr[i-1]], valid when s ≥ arr[i-1]). Base dp[·][0] = true, dp[0][>0] = false. O(n·target) time, O(target) with a bitset or a descending-s 1D array. (The sheet labels it DP-14; meet-in-the-middle is the alternative for large targets, small n.)

a2z-419.description:
Count the subsets of an array of positive integers whose sum equals a given goal; return the count modulo 10^9 + 7 (Striver DP-16 form: every index-distinct selection counts, including the empty subset when goal = 0).

Same 0/1 table as subset-sum but counting: dp[i][s] = dp[i-1][s] + dp[i-1][s - arr[i]] (ways skipping + ways taking). O(n·goal) time, O(goal) space rolling row. Zeros in the input double the counts per zero — the DP handles them naturally.

examples.explanation: {first 2, 3}, {second 2, 3} and {1, 2, 2} — the two 2s are distinct elements, counted by index.

a2z-420.description:
Partition an array of non-negative integers into two subsets S1 and S2 so that S1 - S2 = given difference (S1 ≥ S2); count the number of ways, modulo 10^9 + 7.

Let total = Σarr. S1 + S2 = total and S1 - S2 = d ⇒ S2 = (total - d)/2 — so the problem *reduces* to counting subsets with sum (total-d)/2, the previous exercise, when (total - d) is even and non-negative; otherwise 0. The all-zero subtlety: zeros can join either side, so each zero doubles the count (or let the DP handle them naturally: a zero adds dp[s] to itself → ×2 per zero). O(n·total/2).

examples.explanation: S2 target = (7-1)/2 = 3: subsets {3}, {1a, 2}, {1b, 2} — each defines one partition.
(3-2) is odd — no integer S2 sum exists.

a2z-425.description:
Unbounded knapsack: given n item types (value, weight) and capacity W, maximize total value using any number of copies of each type without exceeding weight. Return the maximum value.

dp[w] = max over items i with weight_i ≤ w of dp[w - weight_i] + value_i — the *same row* feeds itself (that is what 'unbounded' means: take item i, stay able to take it again), so the w-loop ascends and the item-loop may be either order (dp over capacities with inner item scan). O(n·W). Contrast with 0/1 knapsack where ascending w is forbidden. A dominated item (≥ weight, ≤ value) can be pruned first.

examples.explanation: Capacity need not be saturated: three copies of the (w 3, v 50) item use weight 9 for value 150, beating 3+3+4 = 10 weight with value 140.

a2z-426.description:
Rod Cutting (DP-24): a rod of length n must be cut into integer-length pieces; price[i] is the selling price of a piece of length i (i = 1..n, given 1-indexed or as a value array for lengths 1..n). Maximize the total revenue. (Equivalently: unbounded knapsack with weight = value-index = length.)

Revenue(len) = max over first cut k = 1..len of price[k] + Revenue(len - k), with Revenue(0) = 0 — O(n²) tabulation. The identity cut (sell the whole rod) is always a candidate, so an optimal solution may cut zero pieces. The sheet also frames the equivalent form where piece i has length cut[i] and value price[i] — then it is literally unbounded knapsack over capacities 1..n.

examples.explanation: Eight length-1 pieces: 8 × 3 = 24, which beats 2+6 (22) and 4+4 (18).

constraints: O(n²) time, O(n) space; prices non-decreasing is NOT assumed

a2z-429.description:
Find the length of the longest common substring of two strings s1 and s2 — contiguous, unlike the subsequence variant.

DP on suffixes: dp[i][j] = length of the longest common substring *ending at* s1[i-1] and s2[j-1]; if characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1, else 0 (a mismatch kills the run — the difference from LCS-subsequence). Answer is the table maximum. O(n·m) time; rolling row (or single array with a saved diagonal) gives O(m) space; the answer position reconstructs the substring itself.

examples.explanation: "jkl" is the longest shared block ("ab" only reaches 2).
"eeksforgeek" occurs contiguously inside s1 starting at index 1.

constraints: O(n·m) time; O(min(n,m)) space with rolling row

a2z-444.description:
Print a Longest Increasing Subsequence of an array — strictly increasing, not necessarily contiguous — not just its length. If several LIS exist, any one may be printed (lengths equal).

Two routes: (1) O(n²) DP with parent pointers: dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j] over j < i with arr[j] < arr[i], keep prev[i] = winning j, then follow parents from the best end index and reverse; (2) O(n log n) patience sorting: maintain tails[] with binary-search replacement, store the predecessor index at each insertion, and reconstruct by walking the recorded tails' parent chain from the last replaced position. Both must actually emit the sequence.

examples.explanation: Strictly decreasing arrays have no increasing pair.

constraints: 1 <= n <= 10^5 (need the O(n log n) variant) or 10^3 for the quadratic version
Values are integers, duplicates allowed (strict increase)
Print one valid LIS; length must be maximal

a2z-448.description:
Longest bitonic subsequence: a subsequence that first strictly increases and then strictly decreases — with the peak counted once, and purely increasing/decreasing cases allowed (they degenerate to the LIS). Return its maximum length.

Compute forward LIS lengths lis[i] (longest increasing run ending at i) and backward lengths lds[i] (longest decreasing run starting at i, i.e. LIS scanning right-to-left), via the O(n²) DP or O(n log n). Every index is a candidate peak: answer = max over i of lis[i] + lds[i] - 1. Bitonic *subsequence*, not substring.

examples.explanation: The whole array is bitonic with peak 5.
1 → 2 → 10 → 45 → 5 → 2 → 1: lis(45) = 4, lds(45) = 4, minus the shared peak.

constraints: Array values positive integers, duplicates allowed

a2z-450.description:
Given the dimension array arr[0..n-1] — n matrices M_i of size arr[i] × arr[i+1] — find the minimum number of scalar multiplications needed to compute the product, choosing the parenthesization. (Matrix Chain Multiplication, top-down.)

Cost of multiplying p×q by q×r is p·q·r. dp(i, j) = min over split k of dp(i,k) + dp(k+1,j) + arr[i-1]·arr[k]·arr[j] for the range M_i..M_j (1-indexed matrices), base dp(i,i) = 0. Memoized recursion O(n³); the order of multiplication matters enormously — 10×30, 30×5, 5×60: (AB)C costs 1500+3000 = 4500 vs A(BC) 18000+1500 = 19500, a 4.3× gap.
constraints: O(n³) DP with memo; answer fits 64-bit

a2z-451.description:
Matrix Chain Multiplication, bottom-up (DP-49): same cost problem as the top-down version — minimum scalar multiplications to parenthesize n matrices with dimensions arr — implemented as tabulation instead of recursion, and typically also asked alongside printing the optimal parenthesization via a split table.

Fill by chain length: for len = 2..n, for i descending (or ascending) with j = i+len-1, dp[i][j] = min over k in [i, j) of dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + arr[i-1]·arr[k]·arr[j]). The length-major loop guarantees every sub-range is solved before its parent. Store argmin k in a split matrix and emit parentheses with a recursive print(split, i, j). Bottom-up removes stack depth and matches the memo version's O(n³).
constraints: O(n³) tabulation; length outer, start inner; split table for reconstruction
